procedural_history.originating_court: High Court of Punjab and Haryana at Chandigarh
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 29.01.2018 of the High Court of Punjab and Haryana at Chandigarh in CRM– 32387 of 2015 in CRA-S-840-SB of 2015.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court allowed applications for suspension of sentence, preferred by the accused-respondents under Section 389 Cr.P.C., and directed their release on bail while their Appeals were pending in the High Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The State appealed to the Supreme Court, being aggrieved by the High Court's order to suspend the sentences and grant bail to the accused-respondents. The Supreme Court found the High Court's order unsustainable in law, set it aside, and directed the authorities to take the accused-respondents into custody.

decision.sentence_status: Suspension of sentence and grant of bail set aside
directions: The impugned order passed by the High Court is hereby set aside.
The concerned authorities are directed to take the accused-respondents herein into custody forthwith.
Pending applications, if any shall also stand disposed of.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in directing the suspension of sentence and grant of bail to the accused-respondents, considering the gravity of the offence alleged against them.

facts: The accused-respondents were convicted by Trial Courts under Sections 21 and 22 of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 (NDPS Act) for being apprehended with “manufactured drugs”.
They appealed their convictions to the High Court and, during the pendency of the appeals, filed applications for suspension of their sentences and for bail.

The High Court granted these applications, reasoning that since the case involved “manufactured drugs”, the accused should have been tried under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, and not the NDPS Act.
law: The Drugs and Cosmetics Act deals with drugs intended for therapeutic or medicinal use, whereas the NDPS Act aims to curb the use of drugs for intoxication or stimulant effects.
The NDPS Act should not be read in exclusion to the Drugs and Cosmetics Act; they are not mutually exclusive.
It is the prerogative of the State to prosecute an offender under the appropriate law.
When deciding an application for suspension of sentence, a court should not make definitive observations on the merits of the main case, especially when the appeal is still pending.
The gravity of the alleged offence is a key factor to consider when deciding on the suspension of a sentence and grant of bail.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court's legal conclusion—that the accused must be tried under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act instead of the NDPS Act—was incorrect and "does not hold good in law."
The Court clarified that the State was justified in prosecuting under the NDPS Act because the accused's actions constituted a prima-facie violation of that Act.

The Supreme Court criticized the High Court for erroneously making observations on the merits of the case while only deciding on an interim application for suspension of sentence, as the main appeals were still pending.
Considering the gravity of the offences alleged against the accused-respondents under the NDPS Act, the Supreme Court deemed the High Court's order to be unsustainable.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court's order directing the suspension of sentence and grant of bail was "clearly unsustainable in law." This was based on the gravity of the offence and the High Court's flawed reasoning on the merits of the pending appeals. Therefore, the Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order and directed that the accused-respondents be taken back into custody.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in directing the suspension of sentence and grant of bail to the accused-respondents, considering the gravity of the offence alleged against them.
appellant_arguments: The accused-respondents were apprehended in bulk possession of manufactured drugs without any valid authorization, and were convicted by the Trial Court for offences under Section 21 or Section 22 of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 (N.D.P.S Act).
respondent_arguments: The respondents should be tried for the violation of the provisions of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, because the matter deals with “manufactured drugs”.

statutes.act_name: The Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act (N.D.P.S Act)

cases.case_name: Union of India v. Sanjeev V. Deshpande
cases.principle: The N.D.P.S Act should not be read in exclusion to the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, and it is the prerogative of the State to prosecute the offender in accordance with law.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (N.D.P.S.) Act and the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, are not mutually exclusive. It is the prerogative of the State to prosecute an offender under the N.D.P.S. Act for a prima-facie violation of its provisions, even if the substance involved is also a 'manufactured drug' under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act.
obiter: A High Court, when considering an application for suspension of sentence, should not make observations on the merits of the case while the main appeal is still pending before it.

The N.D.P.S. Act does not contemplate framing of rules for prohibiting activities of dealing in narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances, as such prohibition is already contained in Section 8(c) of the Act.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Considering the gravity of the offence, specifically the bulk possession of manufactured drugs without any valid authorization, the High Court's order directing suspension of sentence and grant of bail is legally unsustainable. The High Court's reasoning that the accused must be tried under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, instead of the N.D.P.S Act because they possessed “manufactured drugs”, does not hold good in law, as the action constituted a prima-facie violation of Section 8 of the N.D.P.S Act.
legal_tests_applied: The N.D.P.S Act should not be read in exclusion to the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940.

It is the prerogative of the State to prosecute an offender in accordance with law. Where an action amounts to a prima-facie violation of Section 8 of the N.D.P.S Act, the State is justified in charging the accused under the N.D.P.S Act.
policy_considerations: The State has the prerogative to choose the statute under which to prosecute an offender when their actions violate more than one law.
